title: Mr. Fink, almost quitting trombone, and the jug band
summary: He describes his strict school band teacher, his mother refusing to let him quit in fifth grade, and playing washtub bass and society gigs in high school.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Were you fortunate to have a good teacher in the public school?

Yeah. I’m trying to think. I mean he was like, sorry Mr. Fink, I mean he was cool, he was great. I mean he was a taskmaster. I’ll never forget he had this little like pencil moustache with like the matinee idol kind of guy with the pencil and he was like uh-one-uh-two-uh- three-uh-four, and he’s like looking at you and like this, and with this loud looking

pencil. He was really on it. And yeah, he was a taskmaster. He had my mother and father sign the practice sheet and if I didn’t practice they wouldn’t sign it so he’d know. So it’s a long story. You want to hear that story?
Well go ahead, because I have my own variation.

Well this is fifth grade, and I’m not really serious about it. I had it, and they give you a school instrument. So sometimes I practiced, sometimes I didn’t, and I tried to get my mother to sign one of those weeks where I didn’t and she said, “I’m not going to sign this.” So I said, “I’m going to get in a heap of trouble, come on.” And this was probably halfway through the year, so she said, “No, deal with it.” So I said, “Well then I quit.” And she said, “You can’t quit.” And I said, “Why not?” She said “you deprived someone else from having that trombone so you have to use it the rest of the year and then if you want to quit you can quit.” So I was like, “Awww.” So I continued on and I started practicing more and more, and Mr. Fink at the end of the year they let me take the horn home, I was totally into it by then. And Mr. Fink, he said something to me and I went home and my mother was surprised to see the trombone, and I said, “He said I could have it all summer and that I could play it and use it.” And I said something, I’m paraphrasing or whatever, he said to me, “And Mr. Fink said I might be what you call gifted.” And my mother said she was just, like had a whole batch of tears from laughing. And I still tell that story when she is on one of my gigs. So I say, “It’s all your fault, I could have been a lawyer — I’m Jewish, I could have been a doctor, I could have all this money.” And then in high school I just did everything musical, I would play a washtub bass in a jug band, you know, so my ears opened up early, which is great. I wasn’t just jazz, just jazz, or just one kind of jazz. So I ended up listening to all kinds of stuff and playing in this jug band, we’d do gigs. I remember doing gigs in high school with a local society band, one of the better ones, in New Haven, Connecticut, about a half hour from where I lived. A guy named Pat Dorn. You know it’s funny, I’d always, the joke was I always had a thirty dollar check in my pocket, which was a lot of money back then, or else I didn’t have money. You know like we’d go to a restaurant and I’d say, “I only have this thirty dollar check.”
